title: From Hourly Rate to Annual Salary: How Your Pay Stacks Up Against the NFL Salary Cap
description: Convert your hourly wage to annual pay using the 38-hour week. Compare your earnings to the NFL salary cap and understand tax, super, and minimum wage rules in Australia.
salarySummary: Based on a 38-hour week and 52-week year, your annual gross pay is your hourly rate multiplied by 1,976 hours.

faqs.q: How do I convert my hourly rate to an annual salary?
faqs.a: Multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work each week, then multiply by 52. For a standard full-time week of 38 hours, the formula is hourly rate × 38 × 52. This gives your gross annual pay before tax and super.

faqs.q: Does my annual pay include superannuation?
faqs.a: No. Superannuation is paid on top of your ordinary earnings at 12% (from 1 July 2026). It is not part of your salary. For example, if your annual gross pay is $80,000, your employer must also contribute $9,600 to your super fund, up to the $270,830 maximum contribution base.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the National Minimum Wage and award rates?
faqs.a: The National Minimum Wage is the base rate for award/agreement-free employees. From 1 July 2026 it is $26.44 per hour ($1,004.90 per week). Award rates are higher minimums set for specific industries and occupations. Most employees are covered by an award, which may include penalty rates and allowances.

bodyMarkdown:
## Introduction

Understanding how your hourly rate translates to annual pay is essential whether you're negotiating a salary, planning your budget, or simply curious about where you stand. This guide walks you through the conversion using a standard 38-hour week, explains the role of the National Minimum Wage and award rates, and even draws a comparison to the NFL salary cap—a benchmark often used to gauge top-tier earnings in professional sports.

## How to Convert Hourly to Annual Pay

The basic formula is straightforward: hourly rate × hours per week × 52 weeks. For a full-time employee working 38 hours each week, the annual gross pay equals your hourly rate multiplied by 1,976 hours (38 × 52). This calculation assumes you work the same number of hours every week, with no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, or allowances. If you work part-time or irregular hours, adjust the weekly hours accordingly.

## The 38-Hour Week and the Fortnight

Australia's standard full-time week is 38 hours, as defined by the Fair Work Commission. Many awards and agreements use this as the basis for minimum wages and entitlements. A fortnightly pay period is common, so you can also calculate your fortnightly pay as weekly pay × 2. For example, at the National Minimum Wage of $26.44 per hour, your weekly pay is $1,004.90 and your fortnightly pay is $2,009.80 before tax.

## National Minimum Wage and Award Rates

From 1 July 2026, the National Minimum Wage is $26.44 per hour or $1,004.90 per week for 38 ordinary hours. This is the minimum for award/agreement-free employees. However, most workers are covered by an award or enterprise agreement that sets higher rates. The Fair Work Ombudsman provides pay guides for each award, listing minimum pay rates, allowances, and penalty rates. Always check the applicable award to ensure you're receiving the correct pay.

## Casual Loading and Superannuation

Casual employees are entitled to a 25% loading on top of the minimum wage, making the casual rate $33.05 per hour. This loading compensates for the lack of paid leave and other entitlements. Superannuation guarantee contributions are paid on top of your ordinary earnings at 12% (from 1 July 2026). Super is not deducted from your salary; it is an additional payment your employer makes to your super fund, up to the $270,830 maximum contribution base. For example, if your annual gross pay is $80,000, your employer must contribute $9,600 to super.

## Comparing Your Pay to the NFL Salary Cap

The NFL salary cap is a team-level limit on player salaries, often used as a benchmark for high earnings in professional sports. While it doesn't directly apply to individual Australian workers, it provides an interesting comparison point. For 2026, the NFL salary cap is around $255 million per team. If you divide that by 53 players, the average annual player salary is roughly $4.8 million. That's far above the average Australian full-time adult ordinary time earnings of $108,352 per year (based on ABS Average Weekly Earnings of $2,083.70 per week in May 2026). The NFL salary cap illustrates how top-tier professional athletes' pay dwarfs typical Australian wages, but the conversion principles remain the same: hourly rates, weekly hours, and annual totals.

## Tax and Medicare Considerations

Your annual gross pay is not what you take home. The Australian Taxation Office applies a progressive tax scale for 2026–27: nil tax up to $18,200, 15% from $18,201 to $45,000, 30% from $45,001 to $135,000, 37% from $135,001 to $190,000, and 45% above $190,000. Medicare levy of 2% generally applies. The tax-free threshold means the first $18,200 is tax-free. Use [the timesheet](/) to estimate your take-home pay after tax and Medicare. Remember, this is an estimate only and does not include HELP repayments, Medicare levy surcharge, or salary packaging.

## Conclusion

Converting your hourly rate to annual pay is a simple but powerful tool for understanding your earnings. Whether you're comparing to the NFL salary cap or checking your award entitlements, the formula remains the same. Always verify your pay against the relevant award or agreement, and remember that super is paid on top. For more detailed information, refer to [pay guides](/blog) from the Fair Work Ombudsman or consult [reference tables](/data) for tax and super rates.
